video_title: Trump Is Building an AUTOCRACY | Anne Applebaum on Putin, Kushner, and America’s Future
gist: Anne Applebaum argues Trump's second-term foreign policy has been privatized into a transactional, revolutionary project serving allied business interests (Gulf investments in Kushner, Witkoff/Kushner deal talk with Russia, Brazil tariffs, Venezuelan oil), backed by openly monetized access, pardons and non-enforcement of FCPA. She warns tech platforms' algorithmic and surveillance power, DOJ lawfare and midterm manipulation point to gradual slide into illiberal democracy, with elevated geopolitical risk (Ukraine, Taiwan, North Korea) through 2028.

insights.claim: Applebaum argues US foreign policy under Trump's second term now serves private business interests on an all-of-government scale, distinct from past episodic abuses like United Fruit in Central America.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Foreign policy outcomes are best predicted by mapping which business allies stand to gain, not by stated strategic doctrine.
insights.quote: what we're seeing now is something different in scale and in the and in the sort of all of government approach

insights.claim: Brazil case: after imposing 50% tariffs on Brazil to favor Bolsonaro over Lula, Washington cut diplomatic channels (a Brazil finance minister meeting with the US Treasury Secretary was cancelled in favor of meeting Eduardo Bolsonaro), and the only working channel became a Brazilian businessman with large US businesses who donated heavily to Trump's inauguration.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Tariff levels and trade relief for countries can hinge on ideological alignment and donor intermediaries rather than economics.

insights.claim: Gulf states adapted fastest to the transactional model: the Saudis invested $2 billion in Jared Kushner's company and Qatar gave Trump a luxury airliner she estimates at about $400 million.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Countries with existing family/business ties (Gulf) gain disproportionate access and deal flow; European democracies are structurally disadvantaged.
insights.quote: the Saudis invested $2 billion in it

insights.claim: In Ukraine talks, envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discuss business deals with Moscow (Arctic minerals, gas), and Russia has persuaded them that accepting its war-ending terms, including Ukraine ceding territory, would unlock a 'cornucopia of deals'; a list of such deals is circulating and was cited by The New Yorker.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Watch for Arctic mineral and Russian gas deal proposals as a leading indicator of US pressure on Ukraine to concede territory.
insights.quote: this cornucopia of deals will be available to you

insights.claim: There is no functioning NSC-style policy process: Marco Rubio is both Secretary of State and national security adviser, Trump decides on the fly without strategy, and lower-level State Department ideologues run day-to-day policy, leaving foreign diplomats unsure whom to talk to.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Policy volatility is structural; official statements from Rubio or State may not predict Trump's decisions.

insights.claim: In Venezuela the Trump administration is now cooperating closely with chavistas on oil deals that may benefit companies close to Trump and corrupt Venezuelan oligarchs, showing enemies are defined by willingness to deal, not ideology.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Venezuelan oil access may open for politically connected firms despite ideological rhetoric.

themes.theme: Global revolutionary movement plus business coalition

insights.claim: Applebaum contends the administration is not isolationist but revolutionary: its ideologues aim to export their revolution by linking the global far right and using US diplomatic and military power for allied companies.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Expect continued interventionism (Iran, Venezuela, Greenland, Canada) rather than retrenchment.
insights.quote: Oh, it's not isolationist at all.

insights.claim: State Department democracy-promotion tools (cultural funding, public diplomacy visits) are now being redirected to promote far-right parties, especially in Europe, that oppose regulation and often have links to the crypto industry.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: European political risk now includes active US support for anti-regulation parties; EU regulatory trajectory could shift.

insights.claim: The business coalition behind this foreign policy includes tech companies with global interests, crypto firms seeking to avoid regulation abroad, mineral mining companies seeking deals, and oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: These four sectors are the likeliest beneficiaries of US diplomatic leverage abroad.

insights.claim: The administration treats European liberal democrats, including center-right Christian Democrats, as enemies, projecting US culture-war categories onto Europe.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Transatlantic friction with mainstream European governments is likely to persist.

insights.claim: China is ambiguous: China hawks remain in the administration but Trump wants deals, and China has more leverage over the US than expected through control of rare minerals.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Rare-earth leverage constrains US hawkishness; US-China outcomes remain unpredictable.

insights.claim: Trump treats Putin as a peer to admire rather than an enemy even as Russia escalates sabotage in Europe (attempted bombing of a Polish passenger train, an armed drone at a German airport, assassination squads, arson), a break with US policy since 1945.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: European security risk is rising while US deterrence commitment weakens, supporting European defense spending.

themes.theme: Monetized access and dismantled anti-corruption rules

insights.claim: World Liberty Financial, the president's crypto company, initially accepted anonymous investments in non-tradeable tokens from anyone worldwide, which Applebaum calls in effect a bribe.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Crypto ventures tied to the president function as access channels, raising regulatory and reputational risk for the sector.
insights.quote: literally you were just putting money in a box

insights.claim: Access is openly for sale via inauguration donations, the White House ballroom donations, high-priced Mar-a-Lago dinners, and a market for pardons with known prices and specialized Washington lawyers.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Legal/lobbying intermediaries for pardons and access are a new growth niche; impunity is purchasable.
insights.quote: everybody knows there's a certain price if you want a pardon

insights.claim: The DOJ said it will not enforce the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and the administration blocked the Biden-era rule requiring registration of anonymously owned companies.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Reduced FCPA risk lowers compliance cost for US firms abroad but increases counterparty and governance risk.

insights.claim: She traces the deeper roots to Citizens United, noting no other democracy has campaigns spending hundreds of millions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Structural money-in-politics enables the current scale of influence buying.

insights.claim: China pioneered integrated surveillance in Xinjiang (mandatory 'nanny apps', electricity-usage monitoring) linking cameras, credit cards and social media for real-time tracking and pre-emptive sentiment analysis, and exports the technology to extend influence.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Surveillance tech export is a geopolitical lever and a template for other states.

insights.claim: ICE uses vehicle-mounted cameras with facial recognition linked to databases to identify immigrants on the street; Applebaum warns the same stack could flag critics of the president, and no one in power is pushing to regulate surveillance tech like Flock cameras or license-plate tracking.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Surveillance vendors face little US regulatory risk near term but rising political/backlash risk later.

insights.claim: Tech companies hold more political power than Gilded Age moguls like Standard Oil or JP Morgan because they control the information space via algorithms and surveillance, so politicians fear being suppressed, not just defunded.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Platform algorithm control is a political chokepoint, explaining weak appetite for tech/AI regulation.

insights.claim: Engagement-optimized algorithms favor outrage and extremist rhetoric on both left and right, amplifying radicals over centrists like Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger, and the Republican party has reshaped itself to accommodate this.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Polarization is structurally reinforced by platform incentives.

insights.claim: The DOJ and FBI are being used against Trump's enemies without clear crimes (e.g., Comey), with notable DOJ retirements and refusals acting as remaining checks; CNN, MS Now and Politico were banned from the White House.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Legal harassment raises the cost of dissent even absent convictions.
insights.quote: if you're being investigated by the Department of Justice, your life is hell

insights.claim: Applebaum sees open efforts to manipulate the 2026 midterms via redistricting, mail-ballot disruption, ID requirements (e.g., passports and marriage licenses), and possible ICE/FBI presence on election day.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Election-integrity disputes are a key political risk around November 2026.

insights.claim: A Democratic midterm win would restore congressional oversight, budget and impeachment leverage, and puncture the administration's aura of inevitability, emboldening fence-sitters domestically and abroad.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: A wave election is a regime-shift signal for policy predictability and institutional pushback.

insights.claim: Even with a Democratic win, the next two years could be dangerous because adversaries may see a window before 2028; she flags Europe/Ukraine, Taiwan and North Korea.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Elevated geopolitical tail risk through 2028, particularly Taiwan and Eastern Europe.

insights.claim: Modern democracies decline gradually via elected leaders hollowing institutions (Venezuela under Chávez, Hungary until a wave election ousted its 16-year leader), so the risk is waking up to an irreversible illiberal democracy rather than a coup.
insights.speaker: Anne Applebaum
insights.so_what: Track incremental institutional erosion rather than waiting for a discrete break.
insights.quote: The danger is that the decline will happen slowly and we will suddenly wake up and realize it's, you know, it's not fixable.
